ety.text: First at end of 16th century; borrowed from Middle French estimer, borrowed from Latin aestimō. See estimate and aim, an older word, partly a doublet.

senses.d: Assessment, estimation, or regard; especially; favourable estimation or regard.
ex: We hold her in high esteem.
Many liqueurs, among them chartreuse and benedictine, have long been held in great esteem as aphrodisiac aids.

senses.d: To set a high value on; to regard with respect or reverence.
ex: Will he esteem thy riches?
You talk kindlier: we esteem you for it.

senses.d: To regard something as valuable; to prize.
To look upon something in a particular way.
ex: Thou shouldest (gentle reader) esteem his censure and authority to be of the more weighty credence.
Then he forsook God, which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation.

senses.d: To judge; to estimate; to appraise
ex: The Earth, which I esteem unable to reflect the rays of the Sun.

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin aestimātus, perfect passive participle of aestimō (“to estimate”) (see -ate), older form aestumō (“to value, rate, esteem”); from Old Latin *ais-temos (“one who cuts copper”), meaning one in the Roman Republic who mints money. senses.d: A rough calculation or assessment of the value, size, or cost of something.

senses.d: To judge and form an opinion of the value of, from imperfect data.
ex: It is by the weight of silver, and not the name of the piece, that men estimate commodities and exchange them.
